These exercises let you practise the verbs from the *Data Analysis 1* part of the course book: `select()`, `slice()`, `arrange()`, and the pipe `|>`. They all use the same `titanic_df` dataset from the course.

Write your code in the box, then click **Run Code** to see the result and get feedback.

The last two exercises are a bit more of a stretch - come back to them once you're comfortable with the rest.

## Exercise 1: `select()`

Select the `name`, `age`, and `sex` columns from `titanic_df`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_1
#| setup: true
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yann-ryan/infovis-course/master/titanic_df_full.csv"
download.file(url, "titanic_df.csv")
titanic_df <- read_csv("titanic_df.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_1
titanic_df |> ______
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_1" }
Use `select()`, and list the three column names separated by commas.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_1" }
#### Solution

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_1
#| solution: true
titanic_df |> select(name, age, sex)
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_1
#| check: true
gradethis::grade_this({
  pass_if_equal(explanation = "Nicely done - that's the right three columns.")
  fail("Check that you've selected exactly the `name`, `age`, and `sex` columns (in any order).")
})
```

## Exercise 2: deselecting a column

Select every column from `titanic_df` **except** `cabin`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_2
#| setup: true
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yann-ryan/infovis-course/master/titanic_df_full.csv"
download.file(url, "titanic_df.csv")
titanic_df <- read_csv("titanic_df.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_2
titanic_df |> ______
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_2" }
Put a minus sign directly in front of the column name inside `select()`.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_2" }
#### Solution

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_2
#| solution: true
titanic_df |> select(-cabin)
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_2
#| check: true
gradethis::grade_this({
  pass_if_equal(explanation = "Correct - every column except cabin.")
  fail("Not quite. Remember a minus sign in front of a column name removes it from the selection.")
})
```

## Exercise 3: `starts_with()`

Select all the columns whose names start with the letter `s`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_3
#| setup: true
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yann-ryan/infovis-course/master/titanic_df_full.csv"
download.file(url, "titanic_df.csv")
titanic_df <- read_csv("titanic_df.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_3
titanic_df |> ______
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_3" }
Use the tidyselect helper `starts_with()` inside `select()`.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_3" }
#### Solution

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_3
#| solution: true
titanic_df |> select(starts_with("s"))
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_3
#| check: true
gradethis::grade_this({
  pass_if_equal(explanation = "That's it - survived, sex, and sibsp.")
  fail("Not quite. Check which column names actually start with 's'.")
})
```

## Exercise 4: `slice()`

Select the **first 10 rows** of `titanic_df`.

```{webr}

#| setup: true
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yann-ryan/infovis-course/master/titanic_df_full.csv"
download.file(url, "titanic_df.csv")
titanic_df <- read_csv("titanic_df.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_4
titanic_df |> ______
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_4" }
`slice()` takes a range like `1:10`.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_4" }
#### Solution

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_4
#| solution: true
titanic_df |> slice(1:10)
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_4
#| check: true
gradethis::grade_this({

```

## Exercise 5: `slice_max()`

Find the **5 oldest** passengers in the dataset.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_5
#| setup: true
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yann-ryan/infovis-course/master/titanic_df_full.csv"
download.file(url, "titanic_df.csv")
titanic_df <- read_csv("titanic_df.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_5
titanic_df |> ______
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_5" }
You'll need `slice_max()`, with `order_by = age` and `n = 5`.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_5" }
#### Solution

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_5
#| solution: true
titanic_df |> slice_max(order_by = age, n = 5)
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_5
#| check: true
gradethis::grade_this({
  pass_if_equal(explanation = "Correct - those are the 5 oldest passengers.")
  fail("That's not quite the 5 oldest passengers. Have another look at `slice_max()`.")
})
```

## Exercise 6: `slice_min()`

Find the **5 passengers who paid the least fare**.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_6
#| setup: true
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yann-ryan/infovis-course/master/titanic_df_full.csv"
download.file(url, "titanic_df.csv")
titanic_df <- read_csv("titanic_df.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_6
titanic_df |> ______
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_6" }
`slice_min()` works just like `slice_max()`, but the other way round. Use `order_by = fare` and `n = 5`.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_6" }
#### Solution

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_6
#| solution: true
titanic_df |> slice_min(order_by = fare, n = 5)
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_6
#| check: true
gradethis::grade_this({
  pass_if_equal(explanation = "Correct - those are the 5 cheapest fares.")
  fail("Not quite. Make sure you're using slice_min(), not slice_max().")
})
```

## Exercise 7: `arrange()`, ascending

Sort `titanic_df` by `age`, **youngest first**.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_7
#| setup: true
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yann-ryan/infovis-course/master/titanic_df_full.csv"
download.file(url, "titanic_df.csv")
titanic_df <- read_csv("titanic_df.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_7
titanic_df |> ______
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_7" }
`arrange()` sorts ascending (smallest first) by default - you don't need any extra symbols here.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_7" }
#### Solution

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_7
#| solution: true
titanic_df |> arrange(age)
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_7
#| check: true
gradethis::grade_this({
  pass_if_equal(explanation = "That's it - youngest passengers first.")
  fail("Not quite - check whether you need a minus sign here or not.")
})
```

## Exercise 8: `arrange()`, descending

Sort `titanic_df` by `fare`, from **highest to lowest**.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_8
#| setup: true
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yann-ryan/infovis-course/master/titanic_df_full.csv"
download.file(url, "titanic_df.csv")
titanic_df <- read_csv("titanic_df.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_8
titanic_df |> ______
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_8" }
To sort descending, put a minus sign in front of the column name.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_8" }
#### Solution

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_8
#| solution: true
titanic_df |> arrange(-fare)
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_8
#| check: true
gradethis::grade_this({
  pass_if_equal(explanation = "That's it - sorted from highest to lowest fare.")
  fail("Not quite - remember arrange() sorts ascending unless you tell it otherwise.")
})
```

## Stretch exercise 9: combining verbs with the pipe

In **one** piped sequence, starting from `titanic_df`: keep only the `name`, `pclass`, and `fare` columns, and sort the result by `fare`, from highest to lowest.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_9
#| setup: true
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yann-ryan/infovis-course/master/titanic_df_full.csv"
download.file(url, "titanic_df.csv")
titanic_df <- read_csv("titanic_df.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_9
titanic_df |>
  ______ |>
  ______
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_9" }
You'll need two verbs chained together with `|>`: one to keep the three columns, and one to sort them. The order you do them in doesn't matter here.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_9" }
#### Solution

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_9
#| solution: true
titanic_df |>
  select(name, pclass, fare) |>
  arrange(-fare)
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_9
#| check: true
gradethis::grade_this({
  pass_if_equal(explanation = "Great work - you've combined select() and arrange() in a single pipe.")
  fail("Not quite. You need both the three right columns *and* the right sort order.")
})
```

## Stretch exercise 10: a longer pipeline

Starting from `titanic_df`, in **one** piped sequence: find the **10 passengers who paid the highest fare**, keep only the `name`, `pclass`, and `fare` columns, then sort the result first by `pclass` (ascending), and then by `fare` (descending) *within* each class.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_10
#| setup: true
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yann-ryan/infovis-course/master/titanic_df_full.csv"
download.file(url, "titanic_df.csv")
titanic_df <- read_csv("titanic_df.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_10
titanic_df |>
  ______ |>
  ______ |>
  ______
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_10" }
Three verbs this time: `slice_max()` to get the top 10 fares, `select()` to keep the three columns, and `arrange()` with **two** column names to sort by class then fare. Remember you can list more than one column in `arrange()`, separated by a comma.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_10" }
#### Solution

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_10
#| solution: true
titanic_df |>
  slice_max(order_by = fare, n = 10) |>
  select(name, pclass, fare) |>
  arrange(pclass, -fare)
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_10
#| check: true
gradethis::grade_this({
  pass_if_equal(explanation = "Excellent - that's a proper multi-step pipeline, well done!")
  fail("Not quite there. Check each step separately: the 10 highest fares, the right three columns, then sorted by pclass and -fare together.")
})
```
